title: Row-level security: a predicate that shows each region its rows
objective_text: Write the security predicate that lets each person see only the sales rows of the regions they're mapped to, with an all-regions mapping for managers and nothing for anyone unmapped.
scenario: The sales table is about to be shared with the regional teams. A mapping table says who may see which region; a manager's '*' means every region. Sign-in returns names as people typed them, so 'Ana@Example.com' is the same person as 'ana@example.com'. Someone who isn't in the mapping must see nothing, not everything.
verifies: For each of four sign-ins, the rows the predicate lets through are exactly the rows that person may see, on this PC with DuckDB.
The sales, user_regions and signins tables are as they were: the answer filters rows, it doesn't change the data or the mapping.
does_not_verify: Row-level security in a Fabric Warehouse or the SQL analytics endpoint. There the predicate is an inline table-valued function that a security policy applies to every query, and USER_NAME() supplies the signed-in name; here a DuckDB macro stands in for the function and a table of sign-ins stands in for USER_NAME().
That the rule is enforced for every query path: this lab checks what the predicate returns, not a security policy that applies it.
Column-level, object-level or OneLake folder security, which the same objective also covers.

expected.description: Columns user_name, sale_id, region: the rows each of the four sign-ins may see, ordered by user_name then sale_id.

validation.pass: Each person sees exactly their regions' rows.
validation.fail: Someone sees rows they shouldn't, or misses rows they should: check the manager, the capitalised name and the unmapped person.

validation.pass: The data and the mapping are untouched.
validation.fail: The answer changed a table; row-level security filters rows, it never edits them.

hints: Start with one person: which rows of user_regions belong to who? Compare names the way they're stored.
The mapping is stored in lower case and sign-in isn't, so compare m.user_name with lower(who).

A row is visible when a mapping exists for this person and its region is row_region or '*'. EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM user_regions AS m WHERE ...) returns false when there's no mapping at all, so an unmapped person sees nothing.
explanation: A row-level security predicate answers one question per row: may this person see it? Writing it as EXISTS over the mapping table makes 'no mapping' mean 'no rows', which is the safe default. A wildcard row for managers keeps the mapping short, and comparing names in one case avoids locking someone out because sign-in returned their name with capitals. In a Fabric Warehouse the same predicate is an inline table-valued function that a security policy adds as a filter to the table, so SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE on it only see the rows the predicate lets through.
reset: Reset rebuilds the tables from setup.sql and puts the starter predicate back.
review_notes: result_matches reads the answer's last SELECT, so an answer could replace it with literal rows. The starter keeps the SELECT on a view built in setup, and unchanged protects the tables; hard-coding all the rows is the same limit E49 notes.
